question: Does Cauchy's geometry-only mean chord law extend to isotropically and homogeneously placed arbitrary closed-loop trajectories crossing a two-dimensional domain, and what changes when a loop can fit wholly inside it?

key_findings.claim: The mean in-domain arc length of arbitrary closed contours is pi times the explored domain's area divided by its perimeter when no sampled contour can lie wholly inside the domain.
key_findings.evidence: Blaschke's formula gives total arc-length measure S=2*pi*A1*P2 and Poincare's formula gives intersection-count measure Ni=4*P1*P2. Because a closed contour contributes two boundary crossings per in-domain arc, S/(Ni/2)=pi*A1/P1; the trajectory perimeter cancels.

anchors.section: 3, Proof of the mean arc length theorem

key_findings.claim: The invariance has a sharp geometric validity condition rather than a universal size ratio.
key_findings.evidence: For random circles crossing both convex and non-convex USA-shaped domains, simulations with 100,000 contours reach the Cauchy plateau precisely once the circle radius exceeds the largest-inscribed-circle radius; smaller circles can be fully enclosed and the boundary-crossing arc mean decreases toward zero.

key_findings.claim: The theorem is numerically supported for complicated non-convex contour/domain pairs and is reciprocal under exchanging their roles.
key_findings.evidence: Knight-in-rook, ghost-in-Pac-Man, egg-in-chicken, and chicken-in-egg Monte Carlo experiments recover their respective pi*A/P plateaus after the fully-inscribed placement disappears, even though the two reciprocal thresholds and plateau values differ.

key_findings.claim: For small convex loops inside a convex domain, an approximate sub-threshold formula accounts for entirely enclosed trajectories.
key_findings.evidence: Combining Santalo's overlap measure with Poincare's intersection count yields mean crossing-arc length (P1*P2-2*pi*A2)/(2*P1). Rectangle-in-disk and ellipse-in-convex-shape simulations track this prediction well, with discrepancies as the trajectory approaches the domain's scale.

method.core_idea: Express both total in-domain contour length and the number of crossing arcs as rigid-motion-invariant kinematic measures, then take their ratio.
method.mechanism: Uniformly translate and rotate congruent copies of a closed contour. Use Blaschke's formula for integrated in-domain length and Poincare's formula for boundary intersections; exclude zero-intersection copies entirely contained in the domain. For the small-convex-loop regime, partition Santalo's total-overlap measure into enclosed and crossing placements and subtract the enclosed full perimeters.
assumptions: Contour placements are homogeneous and isotropic under rigid transformations.
The explored bounded two-dimensional domain is simple and connected without holes in the stated proof setup.
Contours are closed, finite-length boundaries of planar domains.
The main exact formula conditions on boundary-crossing trajectories and assumes no congruent copy can be fully enclosed.
The sub-threshold derivation assumes convex shapes and loops small enough that crossing placements have the simple two-intersection topology.

techniques.role: Defines a placement distribution invariant to translation and rotation.
Computes total contour length lying inside the explored domain.
Converts boundary-intersection counts into the measure of crossing arcs.
Separates wholly enclosed and partially overlapping convex placements below the invariance threshold.
Tests shape invariance and estimates embedding thresholds on complex silhouettes.

evaluations.setting: Circular loops on convex-hull and non-convex USA domains
evaluations.metric: Mean arc length normalized by pi*A/P versus radius divided by largest inscribed radius
evaluations.result: Rises from zero and reaches a unit plateau when R is at least the maximum inscribed-circle radius

evaluations.setting: Knight/rook and ghost/Pac-Man arbitrary non-convex pairs
evaluations.metric: Normalized mean arc length versus relative contour/domain area
evaluations.result: Reaches the predicted unit plateau once no trajectory can be fully inscribed
evaluations.baseline: Generalized exact formula, with 100,000 random trajectories per experiment

evaluations.metric: Mirrored normalized arc-length curves and maximum-inscription threshold
evaluations.result: Both orientations recover their domain-specific plateau and different geometric threshold
evaluations.baseline: pi*A_i/P_i for whichever shape is treated as the domain

evaluations.setting: Small rectangle in disk and ellipse in arbitrary convex domain
evaluations.metric: Normalized mean arc length across relative area
evaluations.result: Equation 5 closely follows simulation at small size, with visible mismatch near comparable sizes
evaluations.baseline: Piecewise small-loop approximation below the threshold and exact Cauchy value above it

limitations: The theorem is two-dimensional; no derivation or simulation establishes the closed-surface analogue in three or higher dimensions.
Although the prose says arbitrary bounded domains, the proof explicitly restricts the explored domain to a simple connected topology without holes.
Uniform isotropic rigid placements are essential; biased orientation, nonuniform incidence, correlated loops, or anomalous transport can break a geometry-only mean.
The extended formula below the plateau is derived for convex pairs and is only approximate without the stated curvature/single-crossing condition.
Validation is simulation-only, uses stylized silhouettes, and reports no Monte Carlo uncertainty or convergence analysis.
Recovering area-to-perimeter ratio from a mean does not identify area and perimeter separately, and detecting the embedding threshold may require many rare placements.
failure_modes: Entirely enclosed contours are accidentally included in an estimator conditioned on boundary crossings, changing its denominator and interpretation.
A contour crosses a non-convex boundary many times and a numerical pipeline mistakes total interior length for a single entrance-exit arc.
The placement generator is uniform in a parameterization but not in the kinematic translation-rotation measure.
Finite sampling misses the last feasible fully-inscribed placement and estimates the critical size too early.
Using the convex small-loop approximation for multiply connected or highly non-convex shapes produces systematic bias.
reusable_insights: Ratios of invariant aggregate measures can eliminate nuisance properties of a probing trajectory and expose only domain geometry.
State the sampling condition explicitly: a mean over crossing arcs is different from a mean over all placed loops.
Treat the onset of an invariance plateau as a geometric feasibility signal for whether one shape can fit inside another.
Test a geometric estimator with reciprocal shape roles and adversarial non-convex examples, not only circles and convex domains.
open_questions: What is the exact theorem for multiply connected planar domains and closed surfaces in three dimensions?
How robustly can one estimate pi*A/P and the containment threshold from noisy, dependent, or directionally biased physical trajectories?
Can a full arc-length distribution, rather than only its mean, recover richer shape information or distinguish domains with the same A/P?
Is there a general exact below-threshold expression for non-convex shapes with multiple boundary crossings?

competitive_landscape.title: Invariance properties of random curves: an approach based on integral geometry
competitive_landscape.difference: Mazzolo derives geometry-only traveled-length results for broad random curves and discusses finite contours; the reviewed paper specializes the boundary-crossing statistic to arbitrary closed planar contours, isolates the full-containment threshold, and supplies shape-pair simulations.

competitive_landscape.title: An invariance property of diffusive random walks
competitive_landscape.difference: Blanco and Fournier prove mean first-entry-to-exit length invariance for diffusive walks under isotropic incidence; the reviewed theorem concerns rigidly transformed closed loops and the geometric condition under which a loop fits entirely inside.

competitive_landscape.title: Mean path length invariance in multiple light scattering
competitive_landscape.relationship: experimental physical validation of the broader invariance principle
competitive_landscape.difference: Savo et al. vary scattering strength in optical media and validate an open-path transport invariant; the reviewed work proves a planar integral-geometric result for closed contour arcs and explores containment.

competitive_landscape.title: Violation of the mean path length invariance property
competitive_landscape.difference: Tommasi et al. show anomalous transport can violate invariance when homogeneity and isotropy break; the reviewed result likewise depends on a homogeneous isotropic kinematic ensemble but studies a distinct failure caused by wholly enclosed loops.

novelty_assessment: The paper gives a clean closed-contour version of Cauchy's mean-length invariant and makes the containment threshold operational through diverse shape-pair simulations. It is closely adjacent to Mazzolo's integral-geometric random-curve treatment, which the authors acknowledge, so the clearest incremental value is the explicit crossing-arc ratio, containment interpretation, reciprocal examples, and approximate small-convex-loop regime rather than an entirely independent universal-invariance principle.
